It was a real business, with real clients. That is exactly what made it useful.

Rana's trial opened in a Chicago federal court on May 16, 2011. It ran until June 9. His defence said he had been manipulated. He believed, his lawyers argued, that Headley's assignments came from Pakistan's intelligence service, the ISI — not a terrorist group. Prosecutors answered with emails, wiretaps and Rana's own words after his arrest.

The jury split the verdict in two. Not guilty of supporting the Mumbai attacks — the event at the heart of this story. Guilty of supporting the Denmark plot, and of material support to Lashkar-e-Taiba. Judge Harry Leinenweber called it "a dastardly plot" and sentenced him to fourteen years, plus five years of supervised release.

Not convinced enough for Mumbai. Convinced enough for everything around it. And that gap would decide the next fourteen years.

segments.narration_text:
Here is the hinge. In the US, Rana was tried for one specific crime connected to Mumbai — and acquitted. But India's charges were different. Murder. Waging war against the state. Terrorism under Indian law. Same events. Different crimes.

India had issued a warrant in 2018. Then came an odd twist. In 2020, Rana was released early from a US federal prison on COVID grounds. He was free for days. He was re-arrested — this time on India's extradition request, filed formally that June. Rana fought it for nearly five years. A magistrate certified the extradition. An appeals court upheld it. He took it all the way to the Supreme Court. His last argument was that he would face torture in India, in breach of the UN Convention Against Torture. It didn't work.

The Ninth Circuit had already answered the core question. The crimes charged in India, the court wrote, have "elements independent" from those he had faced in America. Justice Elena Kagan turned down his final emergency application in March 2025. In April, the Court dismissed his last petition. No appeals were left. Not one.
